game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Spending Christmas-time closeted in my room, going through people's texts and emails and news articles, all the while trying to single out enemies of the nation while feeling like a God? Count me in! 

Seriously, this was a pretty enjoyable and unique game. I think they nailed the perfect length with the second instalment (which I played first) as I think this was a tad bit drawn out. Although, the story and pacing is taut enough to never let you lose interest and there are enough twists to keep you hooked. 

In the end, it's a well-presented political thriller. Highly recommended if you're looking for something cheap and unique to fill up 5-6 hours of your time!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

I suppose Orwell is too easy. You have a supervisor meant to guide you, not only in Orwell but to guide your progress through the main storyline. It is very easy to just scroll down till you see phrases or words highlighted. Trying to find conflicting datachunks quickly to get past. While there is nothing stopping you, Orwell does try to encourage you to read. The many articles and websites you visit build the world as you continually gain access. In a way, the people you investigate brings you into the world as you unknowingly destroy theirs each datachunk at a time. There has been arguments about taking away the automatic highlighting, as why should you be hired if they have a system that does it, but there is too much that one can assume is needed. It could easily become entering random phrases or words till you get it right. So this way of highlighting does take away this confusion of what is and isn't noteworthy in a wall of text or conversations.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There's limited sounds to Orwell, having background music and computer sounds. The background soundtrack never really changes until something notewrothy and important comes into view. While computer sounds symbolizes actions, such as a sound of a phone for a phone call and a click as datachunks are being entered.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
While you do stare at a screen of your computer, Orwell has an interesting style when it comes to pictures. They build people with polygons. This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Orwell easily runs well. Only having a few seconds of loading in the beginning of each chapter to load everything. There also seems to be a rare bug, not allowing the player to drag or view the preview of the datachunk. Thankfully, the datachunk is not needed to continue with the story, as it persists through the save, so it may only bother those who view it as an important datachunk to include in a profile.

[h1]Revisiting Orwell[/h1]
As said before, Orwell thrives on the first playthrough. After that, you know what's going to happen. You know what choices affects those you were assigned to. That first playthrough may be remembered as you replay, but so everthing major to the story. This is where you should look up guides as more playthroughs are solely for achievements that were off of the course you took. There are a total of three offical endings, all having subtle changed down the road. There's not much replayability but to see the difference the decisions have on the suspects.

[h1]Report[/h1]
+ Art style
+ Convincing characters; can easily be viewed as real people
+ Compelling story

+/- Your choice to see the world of Orwell
+/- Can be seen as constantly holding your hand

- The phone calls and texts are either too slow or too fast. You have to activate the certain call/text for it to start, breaking immersion since no one will wait till you come into the picture. If you are fast enough you can get two calls or texts (or a combination of the two) at the same time since you are likely to look at something else during other playthroughs. 

Orwell is one of those must play games. With the close hitting theme that may soon become reality. With all chapters released, you can easily have 2-3 hours of gamethrough per playthrough depending on how you choose to play. Orwell shows that you are being watched in some ways, even now, and that even you won't have the best interest for others if they have the possibility to be threats to society. Do not be afraid of going into Orwell this late, as I have and I was able to still get the most out of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
As many others have mentioned, an interesting concept. Don't purchase this game looking for a good gameplay experience. This is certainly a visual novel with a little more interaction than usual, closing in on Point & Click Adventure territory.

It certainly has its own contemporary agenda, which they do a fairly good job at conveying. Its execution isn't always the best, some moments fall flat but are remedied by the pacing and -for me, personally- the desire to see what is going to happen next. While short, it offers enough of interest to be worth a purchase (perhaps at a 40-50% discount, depending on your tastes). 

The 'choices' you will encounter in this game usually boil down to 'jump to conclusion' and 'don't jump to conclusion', which can admittedly work out well in some cases. However, there are times where you will encounter unforseen consequences. These can definitely have an impact on how the game progresses, in increments. For the most part you are playing through a story on rails, with only a few forks in the road that eventually lead to the same place, anyways. The biggest choice you will get takes place at the end of the game, where you will most likely arrive after about 4 hours. 

I would say the game is worth playing for its subject matter alone, it stands on its own as an experience. Some food for thought is to be found, as well.

review_text_raw:
Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 312:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (9/10)

[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a tense, thought-provoking surveillance thriller that does more with a few browser tabs and text files than most games do with entire cities. It casts you as a government contractor sifting through personal data to uncover a growing threat—and forces you to wrestle with how much “truth” you really need to keep people safe. It’s slick, unsettling, and surprisingly emotional.

[b]🪬 Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Brilliant UI that doubles as storytelling. The whole game takes place inside a simulated desktop, with tabs for social media, chat logs, police records, and more. But it’s not just aesthetic! It feels like doing a job. Every click, every search result, every drag-and-drop data point creates tension. The interface is intuitive, immersive, and sinister.

[*] Deep moral ambiguity in every decision. Do you report that someone once expressed violent thoughts in a song lyric? Do you include their real name in a classified file? What about the context? The game forces you to make hard calls on limited info, and the consequences are immediate. 

[*] Tightly written and emotionally resonant. Despite being mostly text, the characters come alive through their messages, posts, and private calls. You start to see their contradictions, their fears, their humor. It’s intimate in a way that hits hard when you're the one deciding what gets flagged—and what gets buried.

[*] Great balance of investigation and puzzle-solving. The game isn’t about cracking codes or hacking firewalls: it’s about connecting dots. Who knows who? What’s fact, what’s hearsay, and what might get someone arrested? You feel clever when you catch a subtle connection between a dating profile and a news article. It’s simple but deeply satisfying.

[*] Fantastic pacing and structure. The game unfolds over five episodes, each building tension and complexity. Just when you think you know what’s going on, it flips your assumptions. It’s rare to find a game this compact that still manages to feel complete and impactful.
[/list]

👁️ [b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Limited replay value. While your choices do have consequences, the story arc mostly funnels toward the same endpoint with slight variations. It’s a brilliant one-time experience, but it may not have the branching depth to support multiple playthroughs.

[*] Some plot twists feel a bit on-the-nose. The writing is mostly subtle, but a few characters and twists lean heavily into dystopian clichés. It's forgivable, especially for a debut game, but occasionally the nuance slips.

[*] A bit short. For players used to longer visual novels or narrative-driven games, [i]Orwell[/i] might feel more like an extended episode than a full series. That said, it’s tightly packed and doesn’t waste your time.
[/list]

[/url] Also, please leave a like and visit [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Indie_Gems]IndieGems[/url] and our YouTube channel for more reviews like this one.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

Rating: 8/10

review_text_raw:
[b]”An interactive dystopian detective novel at its best”[/b]
 
[h1]The Good[/h1]
 
Orwell is an electrifying, Orwellian, (surprisingly enough) thriller with exciting twists and turns everywhere you look. The varied choices and the believable medium through which they are presented breathe so much life into the world and its characters. The mechanics, while there aren’t many to play with and master, they are polished and intuitive enough to get the point across in a believable manner. The writing and world building have to carry the game almost entirely and I can gladly say Osmotic Studios has delivered in this regard! Further to add to this, the pacing fits well into a fairly short experience, around 4 hours, which allows for easy and frequent replayability.
The choices you make are integral to the twists and turns you take. The way the choices are handled in Orwell are often left ambiguous with their outcome and effect on the world around you. Even then, every choice you make feels as though it has an impact on the world, no matter how small.
 
[h1]The Bad[/h1]
 
Certain aspects of the game can fell sluggish, such as the tiresome phone call logs and the constant (seemingly) dead ends on web pages. There can be a case made for these moments, however, since they do add to the overall integrity of this fictional world. My only fear is that some players may feel a bit disappointed during these moments that are paced so much slower than the bits in which the player is in direct control.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
You've been selected to help the government of The Nation investigate and gather data on an activist group. You're to use their new mass surveillance software called Orwell.  Your job is to sift through all the data available to you, determine what is important, what is truth, and then submit this to the government.  If you do a good job, you could prevent future terrorism.

The gameplay is pretty basic, feels a lot like just browsing the internet and reading things.  You explore websites, chat logs, phone call transcripts, etc and you use the information within to create profiles on your subjects/targets.  The game tackles the opposing viewpoints on mass surveillance, asking questions like - is it ok to spy on citizens for their own safety even if it's at the expense of some civil rights?  And where does this end?

I really liked the characters in this game, they felt very real to me.  Each with their own personalities, motivations, realistic reactions to the events of the world around them.  The dialogue was interesting to read too, though I felt it sometimes moved along a bit too slow.  I enjoyed digging deep in each person's life, trying to determine their guilt or innocence.  I really liked that the game allowed me to impact events.  I could submit data that would lead to a person's arrest.  I could paint the portrait of events to wrongly accuse someone, or I could save lives by taking a terrorist off the streets.

The game has 5 chapters and took me a little over 5 hours to beat.  Once you've beaten it, a recent patch allows you to go back to any previous chapter to replay it and do things differently if you wish and see how things play out.

I do wish the game was longer.  I wish it allowed me to explore more narratives than simply one activist group's possible involvement in terrorism.  But for what it is, I still liked it immensely and fully recommend it.

review_text_raw:
I make it a point to go into games blind. Once I picked up the first season of Orwell, not knowing what to expect was definitely the right way to go.

From the get-go, the mere concept of Orwell was enough to get me hooked. Looking into the lives of people in secret, acting like Big Brother, it's a concept that isn't explored that much in fiction. There's obviously 1984 by George Orwell, which this game references alot in its achievements, but other than that I can't think of anything else.

Orwell's story is definitely the best part. It's thrilling and engaging, with twists coming when you least expect them. After playing it blind, this is even more emphasized. The choices you make can also have a huge impact on the outcome of the story, which adds replayability to the game. It can get emotional at times, though not in the "oh my god, I'm going to cry" kind of way. More like "oh my god, what have I done?" The story can also be considered a kind of social commentary on the world, especially concerning surveillance and data and the repurcussions of them (Snowden, anyone?)

Orwell doesn't have much going for it in terms of gameplay, it's really just clicking and dragging. That would normally be a problem if there wasn't an engaging story to back it up, which I think I've already established Orwell has. There were some points that felt a bit slow, such as the dialogue sections that you can't skip through. That might have improved the pacing just a bit, but it didn't detract from the overall experience too much. It's also a bit short, taking me only around 3 hours to complete my first playthrough, but with the different choices affecting the story, again, this adds to the replayability value.

Basically, just go play Orwell.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a difficult one to critique because whether or not you like it is mainly dependent on whether you like the narrative and how it is told. I’m not going to pretend that I know a huge amount about a good story well told, so when it comes to my thoughts on said story, take them with a grain of salt. Before I discuss that though, let’s talk about the game a bit.

[h1]“Interactive” Story[/h1]

In context, you are supposed to be a sort of investigator searching for clues about persons of interest via their emails, social media feeds, and phone conversations. I wouldn’t use the word “investigate” to describe the gameplay. Every import piece of information is already highlighted for you and you just need to drag-and-drop them to the appropriate location. When it comes selecting which documents you want to search through, there are indicators that tell which ones have important data-chunks. You don’t really have to read through the documents and phone texts unless you want story context.

This does streamline the gameplay experience, though. With a lot of story based adventure or point-and-click games, there is a risk of getting stuck at one part and losing all immersion in indirection proportion to mounting frustration. Orwell doesn’t have this problem as it is always very clear where you are supposed to look and this keeps a smooth pacing. As I mentioned earlier, this does contribute to the whole experience not feeling much like a traditional game as it feels much more like a guided tour of the characters and narrative progression. Perhaps a system where you have to highlight pieces of text you feel are important, and if you got the right piece then the story could progress? That may have been the original idea, but that could lead to many frustrations if you just barely missed the part of a quote you were supposed to get.

The only real gameplay in here is when there are two pieces of data that conflict with each other and you have to decide which one to submit to your superior. This could come in the form of two phone conversations by a character where one conversation makes him sound violent and the other makes him sound peaceful. Which one you submit will determine if that character gets arrested later in the story. This factors into a bit of a moral choice system regarding whether you try to paint the main characters and virtuous activists or terrorists. I feel an opportunity was missed to have more greatly divergent storylines to make the player feel like they have a real impact on the world. As it stands, your decisions only change minor events and what ending you get, with most of the heavy decision making existing in the last episode only.

[h1]Interactive “Story”[/h1]

With everything I’ve had to say about the gameplay thus far, you may be a bit perplexed as to why I recommend Orwell. Once again, this isn’t a typical [i]game[/i]. It’s a story with a bit more user control over the pace at which you progress through it. So how is the story?

Pretty good, actually.

The subject matter: government surveillance, is very topical and the game does a good job of showing the many different angles and opinions that people have about it. From those that try to peacefully discuss the issue, publicly criticize it, or are indifferent to it, every character seems believable and for the most part are consistent. The plot is revealed at a steady pace and is able to constantly engage. Appropriate music cues help to reinforce when something drastic has just taken place or when a particularly important piece of data is discovered and it does a good job of drawing you in. The last episode starts to deteriorate when the story starts to massively diverge and the amount of documents and computers to search through becomes overwhelming compared to the rest of the story.

While the data chunks are the most important piece of the story, there is a lot of text to sift through and it fleshes out the characters and game world quite well. A lot of it is unnecessary and for a while I thought that a small sub-plot about terrorism in another country was going to turn out to be a major plot device because the game kept bringing it up, but that ended up being nothing important. Also, documents and conversations are never deleted, so you are free to browse through them at your leisure and one small link could lead you down a rabbit’s hole worth of information. Having assessed these can be handy if the story calls for you to investigate those links and you’re already familiar with them, which does occasionally make you feel like a real investigator.

There are a few off moments when the characters don’t feel believable because we only see them communicate via text. Towards the end, [spoiler]everyone is panicking because they have discovered the Orwell system and can’t figure out how to deal with it,[/spoiler] and sometimes text just isn’t the best way to convey those sorts of emotions. These are hardly deal breakers though because what it boils down to is that whenever I would start the game up, it wasn’t because I felt some obligation to finish it. It was because I wanted to know what happens next. And no matter how many trivial nit-picks I have with the story, that single fact means I have to acknowledge that the story is engaging.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Orwell is a story, and not much of a game. Whatever gameplay is present serves entirely to incrementally progress you through the story and not present any kind of and challenge by itself. An experience like this lives and dies on whether or not its story is engaging which, to me at least, it certainly was.

Also, documents and conversations are never deleted, so you are free to browse through them at your leisure and one small link could lead you down a rabbit’s hole worth of information. Having assessed these can be handy if the story calls for you to investigate those links and you’re already familiar with them, which does occasionally make you feel like a real investigator. There are a few off moments when the characters don’t feel believable because we only see them communicate via text. Towards the end, [spoiler]everyone is panicking because they have discovered the Orwell system and can’t figure out how to deal with it,[/spoiler] and sometimes text just isn’t the best way to convey those sorts of emotions. These are hardly deal breakers though because what it boils down to is that whenever I would start the game up, it wasn’t because I felt some obligation to finish it. It was because I wanted to know what happens next. And no matter how many trivial nit-picks I have with the story, that single fact means I have to acknowledge that the story is engaging. [h1]Conclusion[/h1] Orwell is a story, and not much of a game. Whatever gameplay is present serves entirely to incrementally progress you through the story and not present any kind of and challenge by itself. An experience like this lives and dies on whether or not its story is engaging which, to me at least, it certainly was.

Fantastic game, I can't praise it enough. Solid story, solid characters and character progression, appealing art style, and perfect general pacing. The soundtrack, works perfectly for it- being that it's essentially a solid, subtle repeat throughout the entire game really makes those times where it picks up stand out and feel that much more important.  I really, really hope to see more from this company. And, admittedly, would love it if this premise is revisited in some way. This is the best game I've played in a long, long time. Exactly what I've been looking for. I just couldn't stop playing. I'm kind of sad that I've completely finished it. 

Issues; 
Some of the dialogue becomes a bit broken depending on your choices. Oftentimes Symes and Delacroix mentioned information that I'd intentionally not given them, later on in the story. This only really becomes noticeable on replay-but it could be worked on. Nothing like this will ever be perfect--I'm never going to seriously complain about a choice game having little issues like this. There's just too much that would have to go into a game with so many variants it to make it possible. 
There were a few lingering spelling/grammatical errors, which, given the nature of the game (Internet, instant messaging/texting), didn't really bother me all that much. (Such as Harrison tried to "fell" instead of flee.) I see these things on real articles, it's no different.
There are some bugs present, but, they're clearly being revised and, honestly, aren't game-breaking at this point.

My personal ideas; I believe there could be a little work done on the pacing of the listener- real-time DOES make it all that much more immersive, but, when it comes to replayabilty, and just the general idea of it most likely having an adult player-base, who may only have an hour or so to play before going back to their day-to-day, I feel like there should be...maybe an additional option in the settings to modify speed or..something? It's easier, and more fulfilling to put a game down for a session if you feel you were able to hit a certain level of 'achievement.' You know, the pleasure centers of the brain and all. Maybe if it were simply a more fluid letter-by-letter or syllabalic instead of by completion of a word? I don't know. 
The only other thing I could possibly suggest, would be for, if ever this title is revisited or turned into a 'series' of sorts, that it be a little more flexible? The ability to freely investigate more than is necessary--even additional people. Perhaps just in a casual sense aside from the story, since there is a necessary feeling of a 'time pinch' in the game itself. I think a lot of the audience are people like me who just like to dig, so the chance to just..index on a larger scale would be quite entertaining. 
And, lastly, the ability to generate more datachunks? This could be messy territory, though. I think this would fall into the 'would require too much forethought to ever be possible' category, but it's an idea nontheless. The system is automated, clearly, but, the evaluator should have an option to deem other things appropriate for investigation. I know there were a few things that I would have loved to have flagged that just weren't an option.

My apologies, I'm just VERY excited and passionate about this title. Guys, play it!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I wish I could give a middle ground recommendation. Story based game, little gameplay, not a bad thing but parts of the story and the execution are a little wonky. The game revolves around you uploading datachunks as they call them to a system for a detective like person, known as an Adviser, to review, these are highlighted pieces of text that maybe useful information, which is the first big problem. Rarely are these datachunks useless information so 90% of the time is ok to just upload the regular "blue" datachunks and at least half of the 10% remaining are incredibly obviously useless or incorrect, although uploading them allow you to see more "related documents" Conflicting datachunks are yellow, tell you and point to their conflicting datachunk where you generally have to make a choice which is correct, and you'll be able to find the information to make the most informed call almost every time. Quite often when uploading a datachunk it will only provide a bit of a picture from the actual uploaded text or picture but the adviser will add significantly more detail to advance the plot than the piece of information should be providing. I'm going to talk very generally about the end, no character names, examples or spoilers. Another wonky component was the final day, each day is the next episode, entering the final day the rules change and you can only upload 20 datachunks, which is a great mechanic and should've been a mechanic the whole way through the game, the reasoning for this change is really awkward because "something, fairly tame" is going to happen at a certain time during the final day, but this was not a concern elsewhere in the game. The final day brings me to the biggest problem with the game, there is a point after uploading the 20 datachunks which kind of transitions the game into the endgame portion, but during this information was revealed that I didn't know and was prevented as if I had found it, which made me feel like the entire sequence isn't heavily effected by the uploaded datachunks, it made the endgame feel very cheap as you start making what should be the very impactful decisions. You basically just select one of the endgame directions after the transition rather than all or most of your game decisions meaning something. The other problem is the ending seems extremely preachy rather than allowing the player to figure out how they feel about the subject matter.

But whats good about Orwell? The characters in general feel much more realistic rather than when you see someone try to write internet conversations and forum posts. Orwell does a pretty good job of leading and misleading you at different points which does make it more interesting. The pacing in phone calls/text chats feel really good and suspenseful, assuming the player can read fast enough to keep up, same goes for connecting documents, although some can feel way too convenient. The concept and questions it should be asking the player about the extent of security and surveillance is excellent.

Would I buy this game for $10? Probably not, it only took 5 hours to complete, including when I walked away for a few minutes. Sale price? Yah its definitely worth checking out. If its under $3 definitely get it, its an interesting ride.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
8/10: A great immersive 'clicking sim' story game, with a couple of rough edges.

The good: I was completely engaged with the game from start to finish (binged it in 1 session). I felt that the difficulty, pacing and depth was just right for most of the game. The fact that the most minor of decisions are final and cannot be undone even though their consequences might not be realized until an hour or two later really kept me on my toes. While most of the game plays like a relaxing interactive story w/o difficulty there was just enough setpiece 'puzzles' (where a key decision required rereading every piece of information thoroughly and thinking hard) to create a good cycle of tension without feeling exhausting. And just when my brain was out of juice, the game ended. Beautiful

The bad: 1) the fact that the 'important information' to your investigation is hard-coded rather than free to deduce by yourself rears its ugly head occasionally. The developer, understandably, didn't account for every permutation that information might be read from. So, for example, when I'm asked to provide a portrait of a target and the game doesn't let me submit that one picture because the dev missed it it was a a little frustrating. It frustrates because, while minor, the immersion drops and the plot's rails become visible for just a second. 

*2 INVOLVES MINOR PLOT SPOILERS* TLDR: meh ending

[spoiler]2) The obligatory *twist ending* was not well executed. I imagine I'm not the first one to pick up on that given how glaringly it stands out from the quality of the rest of the game (can be read as a plus.). Arthur Conan Doyle's (Sherlock Holmes) rules of a good detective story require that the answer be obvious 'had you known X', ie there must be a underlying logic to it that the reader/player was only unable to uncover until the end due to not having all the pieces. The secret villain showed no indication that [hidden] was capable of performing the act even after everything was revealed, which makes the reveal feel like plain shock value. In fact I was absolutely caught off guard by the reveal when it was done through NPC dialog. 

To the devs: Objective fact reveals like "surprise he/she was actually secretly there" or "he/she is acting mysteriously" alone does not convince me that they are secretly the culprit. You gotta show motive, character, drives. Not what they did but why they did it.[/spoiler]

Overall, would absolutely say that the game nailed what it set out to do, i.e. letting you roleplay as a Big Brother spying and tearing through everyone's personal info on a quest to stop terrorism. And the moral of the story was made pretty well: guessing who someone is through their personal info alone without context is inaccurate. That the plot that came attached to that experience, and the human limitations of the dev, is a little underwhelming does not discount the fact that I was completely immersed into it. Which is a rare thing

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell has definitely made it onto my list of indie favorites. One of the most interesting and engaging games I've played in a long time.

[b]Story[/b]
The story and characters are well written, realistic, and relatable. The pacing is perfect and each chapter will leave you anxious to get into the next one. The world has depth and lives and breathes. Your actions feel as though they carry real weight with consequences that follow you. This is the sort of story that you'll think about and speculate about even when you're not playing. It's obvious a lot of thought was put into Orwell.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
I think it's fair to say Orwell is more of an interactive novel than a game. But that by no means is a mark against it.

Gameplay is simple but effective. You play as an investigator trying to solve a recent bombing using whatever online information, public or private, is made available to you. When you come across information that your system (named Orwell) recognizes as relevant to one of your target persons, it becomes highlighted and you can choose to upload it to Orwell's database where your superiors can then see it and act on it.

But this surveillance system isn't perfect. Sometimes conflicting or irrelevant information will be highlighted and you'll have to use your best judgement when choosing what to upload. I won't explain more in depth than that - I think the rest of the gameplay is best experienced when you discover it yourself. But I promise the gameplay isn't the mindless drag and drop that it might seem.

And what I thought was neat is that while some aspects of the gameplay might seem arbitrary or slightly confusing at first, these mechanics have a real canon, in-world explanation that is revealed as you progress. The gameplay really feels like part of the story here.

[b]Performance[/b]
It'll probably run on just about anything.

[b]Length[/b]
There are five chapters, each of which took me 45-60 minutes or so. Some people might complete it faster since I'm the methodical, read-everything-before-moving-on sort (which is rewarding with Orwell). Very little (if any) replay value though. Some people might recommend playing it all in one sitting, but I would say taking day or two long breaks like I did is the way to go.

[b]Price[/b]
Full price at the time of this review is $10. I was able to grab Orwell while it was temporarily free. $10 seems a little bit steep at first, but considering the ~5 hours I got out of it and the impression it left on me, I would say Orwell is easily worth that much. You can probably also count on Orwell going on sale or getting it cheap in a bundle if you're still on the fence.

[b]Conclusion[/b]
Get it. If you enjoy indie games, get it. If you like a good detective story, get it. If surveillance or digital privacy even remotely interest you (which they should), get it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game honestly fucked me up a bit by the end of it.

At first it kinda comes off as a Death and Taxes kind of game, but no. It is one long single story arch that is honestly wonderfully crafted. My investment and intrigue in the game honestly just grew more and more as the game went on and went in turns I didn't expect. I often found myself expecting one culprit only to move on to another and another and another as I found and submitted more evidence.

I played the whole game in 5 hours, but honestly I will go back for more. I have more achievements to get and I want to see what else I can find. I still have a bunch of questions and I want to find the answers!

Game play wise the choice mechanics here are really interesting. Rather than just swipping information away like you do in most games like this, you are given loads of info and can pick and chose information that you submit based on what the system deems relevant for you to possibly submit. Then there are some bits of info that are game changing. You also can't go back and take back previously submitted information, previous info you have supplied can only be updated.

All the info is presented to you in a way that you can just select the highlighted sentences and submit the info. You can submit evidence without actually reading the whole articles or chats or what ever it is that highlighted sentence is in. However, that is because the system only selects what it finds relevant. Sometimes the context surrounding that sentence can drastically change it's implications. Which is an amazing way of proving one of many points in this game. If you look at the small picture and just submit the evidence based on what the system shows you, you will get a lot more things wrong. I know because at first I didn't read statements completely. Then I realized a few times I messed up, I wished I could take something back but I couldn't and slowly I became more cautious of what I submitted. This also applied to times that I submitted fishy or questionable evidence only to realize a few web pages or convos later that the info was inaccurate.

If you like thought provoking story lines. The kind of game that afterwards you question of you did the right things, this is a great game for you. It's slightly slow pacing at first, but if you can get passed that the game will have you hooked. Another good comparison would be that if you are into Black Mirrors on Netflix, this is a game you are sure to enjoy.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: So, Orwell is mixture of good stuff and mediocre stuff. I really like the gameplay, structuring and pacing (both of the plot and the gameplay). The central gameplay loop is basically just looking through various documents and conversations to find information potentially relevant to the investigation. I thought it would be boring at first, but it actually never felt tired, and remains engaging throughout. Gameplay wise, it's pretty good, with only a few minor tweaks that could improve efficiency. The story is where it gets less positive. As you progress through the game, you learn more about the characters, who they are, their background, their personality, etc. etc. This is the strongest aspect of the story, because their well written characters, and seeing them react to what's happening after learning so much about them makes you think really carefully about what you do that might affect them. Unfortunately, these characters all seem fixated on the agenda of beating the message of the game over your head repeatedly. The themes and message? That's where we really start to lose traction. First off, the message is obvious. One of the characters at the end practically spells it out. Thanks, if the all the references to the number 1984 didn't make it obvious, nor the chapters being named after phrases from 1984, then I would of still gotten it from the name and premise. Mass surveillance is bad! Like, really unethical! No, really? I thought that was obvious. For the all the 1984 references though, it doesn't seem like the writers really understood 1984. 1984 isn't about surveillance. It's about the manipulation of thought, primarily through language and media. The surveillance is window dressing. In fact, you never even know if the citizens in 1984 are actually being watched, because it doesn't matter. It just matters that they think they are. I digress. The game also comes as thinking it's a bit smarter than it really is. Despite that, it's never boring, and though a little melodramatic, and the tendency to believe that the player hasn't caught on that mass surveillance is kinda screwed up, I did feel desire to continue, and though the end is also a little silly (It forces you to choose between 3 equally culpable people, for no explained reason. Why can't I incriminate them all?), I didn't feel cheated. I didn't pay I got it for free from humble, but I wouldn't have regretted paying for it. Try episode 1, if you like it, it won't overly disappoint from there, and it'll retain its fun.

Mass surveillance is bad! Like, really unethical! No, really? I thought that was obvious. For the all the 1984 references though, it doesn't seem like the writers really understood 1984. 1984 isn't about surveillance. It's about the manipulation of thought, primarily through language and media. The surveillance is window dressing. In fact, you never even know if the citizens in 1984 are actually being watched, because it doesn't matter. It just matters that they think they are. I digress. The game also comes as thinking it's a bit smarter than it really is. Despite that, it's never boring, and though a little melodramatic, and the tendency to believe that the player hasn't caught on that mass surveillance is kinda screwed up, I did feel desire to continue, and though the end is also a little silly (It forces you to choose between 3 equally culpable people, for no explained reason. Why can't I incriminate them all?), I didn't feel cheated. I didn't pay I got it for free from humble, but I wouldn't have regretted paying for it. Try episode 1, if you like it, it won't overly disappoint from there, and it'll retain its fun.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell : Keeping an Eye on You shows and emphasizes well how much things taken out of their context can be manipulated to say anything and everything. In game, one run after the other, you will always have the very same elements, but you can reach diametrically different conclusions, which gives some replayability to the game (to get all achievements, you'll need at least 3 runs).

Since there is nearly no time pressure (apart from very specific moments), I indulged in reading everything the game had to offer and, following a guide to get all endings, I finished my first run in roughly 4h and subsequent ones in 2h or so.
Fortunately, the game has been translated in multiple languages because some characters mainly use abbreviations, which can make it difficult to understand to any non-native speaker.
Soundtracks do a great job and more than once, there will be these specific ones kicking in whenever you stumble upon a shocking/emotional revelation. And I must admit that some of them gave me the shivers.
This game's aesthetics are very much to my tastes. The low-poly designs are good-looking, and the uncluttered display makes Orwell easy to navigate.

Real-time discussions are interesting at first, and it makes our surveillance feel more fleshed out/real. But at the same time, it really breaks the rhythm and thus the immersion, especially on replay. Even at the highest speed, it is still unbelievably slow and you just can't skip these unsufferable parts. Though, mind that you can go back to specific chapters (it rewrites your progression) for achievement purposes and such. Moreover, once you've opened a real-time discussion, it will keep unraveling even if you don't stay to watch it til the end.
Should you want to be Orwell's E. Snowden, know that you'll need to do a piss-poor job from the very beginning. Yes, even before knowing that there is something wrong here, which makes no sense lore-wise.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a fantastic experience. Orwell is a text-based game with a fairly linear progression. You play an investigator who uses an all-encompassing crowdsources surveillance system called Orwell. You are tasked with uncovering and identifying members of an alleged domestic terrorism group called "Thought" in the fictional country called "The Nation." You work your way through this task by investigating the phone calls, texts, emails, social media, dating profiles, bank information, and relationships of the various "suspects." You take snippets of highlighted information and upload them to Orwell (an irreversable process). It's up to you to decide, at times, which data is relevant. Choose poorly, and you can cause the deaths of certain suspects.

 If you hadn't guessed, this game is like an interactive modern version of the book "1984" by George Orwell (my favorite book of all time, by the way.) It offers a striking glimpse into what a complete surviallance state would look like in the modern world, and what the benfits and pitfuls to such a system may be. The game is pretty short at around 4 hours, but that's really all it needed to be. It definitely lacks replayability, but I don't think the story would have the impact of the first playthrough if I were to play it again. If you're interested in the subect matter or in story-based games in general, play Orwell. If you're looking for action or exploration, seek elsewhere. Just be mindful, because you never know who is watching. 

+Excellent story and pacing
+Haunting music
+UI that is easily navigated
+Expertly written
+Believable characters
+Excellent air of mystery hanging over the story
+Orwellian

-/+ Short game

-Sometimes got stuck, had to search out relevant info for too long
-Lacks replayability

OVERALL:

9.3/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It took me a LONG time to give this game a good look.  I had a low first impression, it looked just a little TOO indie/low-tech.  Don't get me wrong, I like many Indie games but this one seemed just a tad too 'lite'.  The low price of $9.99 enforced that perception.

First it kept appearing in my queue, but I didn't think I'd be interested, so I kept ignoring it.  Next, I finally added it to my wishlist.  Where it remained for at least a year.  Then I finally bought it on sale with a bunch of other stuff so then it just sat in my Library for several months while I played the other stuff first.  Then, the first time I booted it up I just couldn't make sense of what was going on design-wise and I didn't have the patience to figure it out so it sat in my Library for another few weeks.  Finally, the next time I played it, it made much more sense and everything sort of 'clicked' for me.  Now I love it.

Gameplay, pacing, design, story plot, and music are all especially evocative of Introversion Software's excellent indie hacking game Uplink, without the frantic time-is-counting-down aspect of Uplink.  When I play Orwell, I feel like I'm playing Uplink, but it's much brighter and prettier and I'm more relaxed, lol.

I'm glad to see the developers continue to support this game with new episodes being released.  Since the game has no vocal acting and is a basic (but graceful) design, I imagine they could continue to crank out episodes relatively quickly if the demand justifies it.  Which is good because I want more.  The hallmark of any excellent game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Compelling psychological deduction game, piece together information found in newspapers, social media, personal data and prevent a terrorist attack, aka cyber stalking - the game.

The overall theme is not surprising given the title but the story takes some intriguing turns. The pacing worked great for me and the choices you make (the info you upload) have a lasting effect on the story, not just on whether you get "the one good or the one bad ending", so to speak.

You will not always know what the "correct" answer is and it is up to you to decide which often contradictory data chunks are relevant to the case. If you mindlessly upload everything without question and without considering the context, you will probably not have such a good time. 
I would have prefered if the develeopers didn't differetate between blue and yellow data chunks. They aren't that different anyway and I would recommend ignoring the color coding as much as you can.

I can also see this working great in an educational setting or for people who usually don't play video games.

Well-executed, original, creative…

A great marriage between choose your own adventure books, visual novels, and government-mandated homework. If you're interested in a quick dip into the ethics of information surveillance, and if you enjoy text-driven, mostly linear narratives, this is a good game for you.

I'm debating whether or not to call it a "game," since it is more of a visual novel with a creative spin. There are opportunities for choice and failure, but not so much as I would have hoped from a game like this. On a scale of 1 to 10, where 1 is "I'm reading a book" and 10 is "I can do whatever I want", this would probably score a 3. That being said, I still really enjoyed the story, and I commend the developers and writers for great pacing of the story, and the enormously detailed work that went into it.

7/10, would recommend, provided it's your thing.

All in all, definitely a "pleasant" way to spend an evening.
